claim: Major depressive disorder (MDD) affects approximately 16% of the global population at some point in life.
source: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent and potentially life-threatening disorder that affects approximately 16% of the global population at some point in life (Mayberg, 2009; Nestler and Hyman, 2010; Flint and Kendler, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Mayberg, 2009; Nestler and Hyman, 2010; Flint and Kendler, 2014).

claim: Core symptoms of MDD include lack of motivation, reduced ability to derive pleasure from natural rewards (anhedonia) and abnormalities of sleep and appetite.
source: Core symptoms of MDD include lack of motivation, reduced ability to derive pleasure from natural rewards (anhedonia) and abnormalities of sleep and appetite.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge about MDD symptoms.

claim: MDD is thought to occur as a result of combined genetic, environmental, and biological factors.
source: MDD is thought to occur as a result of combined genetic, environmental, and biological factors.
evidence: This reflects established scientific consensus about the multifactorial etiology of MDD.

claim: MDD is characterized by alterations in the activity of a distributed circuit controlling emotive behaviors.
source: Although the nature of these factors and their relative contributions to the disorder remain largely unknown, human studies (Mayberg, 2009; Hasler and Northoff, 2011; Morishita et al., 2014) and circuit-based molecular genetic analysis in mice (Nestler and Hyman, 2010; Li et al., 2012; Tye and Deisseroth, 2012; Svenningson et al., 2006) have shown that MDD is characterized by alterations in the activity of a distributed circuit controlling emotive behaviors
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to human studies and mouse studies.

claim: Treatments that act within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) can have a strong therapeutic effect on MDD.
source: and that treatments that act within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) can have a strong therapeutic effect (Leuchter et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Leuchter et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2012).

claim: Environmental stress, including early childhood trauma and recent stressful experiences, can contribute to MDD.
source: It is widely recognized that environmental stress, including early childhood trauma and recent stressful experiences, can contribute to MDD (Russo et al., 2012; McEwen and Morrison, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Russo et al., 2012; McEwen and Morrison, 2013).

claim: Depressive behaviors can be elicited in experimental animals using a variety of stressors.
source: Depressive behaviors can be elicited in experimental animals using a variety of stressors, which typically induce alterations in neuronal morphology and synaptic function (Shansky and Morrison, 2009; Moench and Wellman, 2014) in the mPFC
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Shansky and Morrison, 2009; Moench and Wellman, 2014).

claim: Stressors typically induce alterations in neuronal morphology and synaptic function in the mPFC.
source: Depressive behaviors can be elicited in experimental animals using a variety of stressors, which typically induce alterations in neuronal morphology and synaptic function (Shansky and Morrison, 2009; Moench and Wellman, 2014) in the mPFC
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Shansky and Morrison, 2009; Moench and Wellman, 2014).

claim: Thinning of the mPFC occurs in MDD.
source: that are consonant with the thinning of the mPFC that occurs in MDD (Kroes et al., 2011; Grieve et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Kroes et al., 2011; Grieve et al., 2013).

claim: Inactivation of the ventral mPFC results in loss of cortical control of stress.
source: Inactivation of the ventral mPFC results in loss of cortical control of stress (Diorio et al., 1993; Figueiredo et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Diorio et al., 1993; Figueiredo et al., 2003).

claim: Inactivation of the ventral mPFC alters the activation of brainstem neurons that regulate behavioral responses to stress.
source: and alters the activation of brainstem neurons that regulate behavioral responses to stress (Maier, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maier, 2015.

claim: Optogenetic activation of mPFC neurons projecting to the dorsal raphe nucleus can reversibly alter mobility in the forced swim test.
source: Optogenetic activation of mPFC neurons projecting to the dorsal raphe nucleus can reversibly alter mobility in the forced swim test (FST), implicating this specific class of pyramidal cells in the behavioral responses to stressful situations (Warden et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Warden et al., 2012.

claim: Studies of Wolfram syndrome have identified Wfs1 as a clear example of a gene that can cause MDD in humans.
source: Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have demonstrated that common depression is likely to result from alterations in a very large number of genes of small effect (Flint and Kendler, 2014), studies of Wolfram syndrome have identified Wfs1 as a clear example of a gene that can cause MDD in humans (Swift et al., 1990; Crawford et al., 2002; Swift and Swift, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Swift et al., 1990; Crawford et al., 2002; Swift and Swift, 2005).

claim: Common depression is likely to result from alterations in a very large number of genes of small effect.
source: Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have demonstrated that common depression is likely to result from alterations in a very large number of genes of small effect (Flint and Kendler, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Flint and Kendler, 2014.

claim: Wfs1 is expressed in a specific population of neurotrophin 3 (Ntf3) and proenkephalin (Penk1) expressing pyramidal cells in superficial layer 2/3 of the mPFC.
source: Here, we have employed bacTRAP translational profiling and virus mediated trans-synaptic tracing studies (Wall et al., 2010) to demonstrate that the Wolfram syndrome gene (Wfs1) is expressed in a specific population of neurotrophin 3 (Ntf3) and proenkephalin (Penk1) expressing pyramidal cells in superficial layer 2/3 of the mPFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own experimental data using bacTRAP translational profiling and virus-mediated tracing studies.

claim: Wfs1-expressing layer 2/3 pyramidal cells receive projections from other cortical structures, from the posterior thalamic nuclear group, and from the lateral amygdala.
source: These cells receive projections from other cortical structures, from the posterior thalamic nuclear group, and from the lateral amygdala.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own viral tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons of conditional knockout mice (Wfs1/CKO) alters stress-induced depression-related behaviors.
source: Deletion of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons of conditional knockout mice (Wfs1/CKO) alters stress-induced depression-related behaviors
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data from Wfs1/CKO mice.

claim: Deletion of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons induces the expression of the immediate early gene Fos in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus.
source: induces the expression of the immediate early gene Fos in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunohistochemistry data showing cFos expression in the PVN.

claim: Deletion of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons results in enhanced accumulation of serum corticosterone.
source: and results in enhanced accumulation of serum corticosterone.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own radioimmunoassay data measuring serum corticosterone levels.

claim: Increased stress-induced depressive behavior is evident in animals from which Wfs1 was deleted specifically in the mPFC.
source: Increased stress-induced depressive behavior is also evident in animals from which Wfs1 was deleted specifically in the mPFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data from Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice.

claim: Wfs1 is present in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of superficial cortical pyramidal cells.
source: Wfs1 is present in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of superficial cortical pyramidal cells
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: Loss of Wfs1 in layer 2/3 neurons results in altered growth factor and neurotrophin processing in response to inescapable restraint stress.
source: and its loss in these neurons results in altered growth factor and neurotrophin processing in response to inescapable restraint stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own Western blot data showing altered WNT7A and proNTF3 levels.

claim: Superficial layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the mPFC play a critical role in stress-induced depressive behaviors.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that superficial layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the mPFC can play a critical role in stress-induced depressive behaviors
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' experimental data showing behavioral changes in Wfs1 knockout mice.

claim: Dysfunction of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons leads to activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and elevated blood corticosterone levels.
source: and indicate that dysfunction of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons leads to activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and elevated blood corticosterone levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own data showing increased cFos in PVN and elevated serum corticosterone.

claim: The major depression evident in patients with Wolfram syndrome and carriers may occur in part due to hyperactivation of the HPA axis in response to stress.
source: They highlight a role for superficial layer 2/3 pyramidal cells of the mPFC in the modulation of depressive behaviors and suggest that the major depression evident in patients with Wolfram syndrome and carriers may occur in part due to hyperactivation of the HPA axis in response to stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the authors' data extrapolated to human patients.

claim: Wolfram syndrome is a complex, multisystem disorder that results in early onset diabetes, optic atrophy, and increased risk for MDD.
source: Wolfram syndrome is a complex, multisystem disorder that results in early onset diabetes, optic atrophy, and increased risk for MDD (Rigoli et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rigoli et al., 2011.

claim: Wfs1 knockout mice accurately model many aspects of Wolfram syndrome, including type 1 diabetes, retinal degeneration, and impaired behavioral responses to stress.
source: Wfs1 knockout mice accurately model many aspects of Wolfram syndrome, including type 1 diabetes, retinal degeneration, and impaired behavioral responses to stress (Luuk et al., 2008; Kato et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Luuk et al., 2008; Kato et al., 2008).

claim: The gene for neurotrophin 3 (Ntf3) is expressed primarily in superficial layers of the prefrontal cortex.
source: we took advantage of ISH data demonstrating that the gene for neurotrophin 3 (Ntf3) is expressed primarily in superficial layers of this region of cortex (Figure 1B) (www.bgem.com).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data from www.bgem.com.

claim: EGFP/L10a expression in the Ntf3 bacTRAP founder line PS1046 was primarily restricted to superficial layer 2/3 in the mPFC, including the prelimbic, infralimbic and medial orbitofrontal regions.
source: EGFP/L10a expression was primarily restricted to superficial layer 2/3 in the mPFC, including the prelimbic, infralimbic and medial orbitofrontal regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of EGFP/L10a was observed only in the NeuN + neurons.
source: Expression of EGFP/L10a was observed only in the NeuN + neurons (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own data, though not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The soma of EGFP/L10a-expressing cells was pyramidal, with a clear apical dendrite.
source: Furthermore, at high magnification, it was evident that the soma of EGFP/L10a-expressing cells was pyramidal, with a clear apical dendrite (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: EGFP/L10a expression was localized to the soma, proximal dendrites, and nucleolus.
source: EGFP/L10a expression was localized to the soma, proximal dendrites, and nucleolus, as described for other bacTRAP mouse lines (Doyle et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own observations and a citation to Doyle et al., 2008.

claim: Ntf3 gene is expressed in a laminar pattern in the cortex.
source: These results confirm previous studies demonstrating laminar expression of Ntf3 gene in the cortex (Vigers et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vigers et al., 2000.

claim: Ntf3-targeted cells are supragranular layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: and identify these cells as supragranular layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' anatomical characterization data.

claim: Ntf3 layer 2/3 pyramidal cells express genes in their ground state that can be used to distinguish them from other cortical cell types.
source: As expected from the anatomical characterization of the Ntf3-targeted cells, comparative analysis of TRAP data collected from these cell types (Shrestha et al., 2015; Doyle et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2012; Nakajima et al., 2014) indicates clearly that Ntf3 layer 2/3 pyramidal cells express genes in their ground state that can be used to distinguish them from other cortical cell types (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own TRAP profiling data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: mRNAs enriched in Ntf3 pyramidal cells include Cux2, Penk, Smoc2, Matn2, Wfs1, Htr5b, Nptx2, Hap1, Gsg1l, and Ntf3.
source: Examination of mRNAs enriched in Ntf3 pyramidal cells (Figure 1G,H; Figure 1—source data 1, 2) relative to those expressed in the entire cerebral cortex reveals a variety of control genes previously shown to be expressed in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells, including Cux2, Penk, Smoc2, Matn2, Wfs1, Htr5b, Nptx2, Hap1, Gsg1l, Ntf3 (www.brain-map.org).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own microarray data and reference to www.brain-map.org.

claim: Laminar markers for cortical layers 4, 5, and 6 were not enriched in Ntf3 cells.
source: Laminar markers that have been reported to be expressed specifically in cortical layers 4 (e.g., Hsd11b1), 5 (e.g., Etv1), and 6 (e.g., Drd1a, Ctgf) were not enriched (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own data, though not shown in the manuscript.

claim: All 9 annotated marker genes for non-pyramidal cells (glial cells and inter-neurons) were depleted in the Ntf3 cells.
source: Of 9 annotated marker genes (Aqp4, Gfap, Aldh1L1, Slc1a3, Olig2, Gad1, Dlx1, Nek7 and Gad2) for non-pyramidal cells (glial cells and inter-neurons), all were depleted in the Ntf3 cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own microarray data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Housekeeping genes (Rps6, Eif4e, Dnm2 and Ttf1) were all expressed within twofold enrichment boundary in Ntf3 cells.
source: Housekeeping genes (Rps6, Eif4e, Dnm2 and Ttf1) were all expressed within twofold enrichment boundary (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own microarray data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR confirmed that Ntf3 (2^-ddCT = 12.09 ± 1.37), Wfs1 (2^-ddCT = 3.07 ± 0.86), and Penk (2^-ddCT = 2.69 ± 0.31) mRNAs are enriched in the Ntf3 cells.
source: and quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) of TRAP RNA provided additional confirmation that Ntf3 (2^-ddCT = 12.09 ± 1.37), Wfs1 (2^-ddCT = 3.07 ± 0.86), and Penk (2^-ddCT = 2.69 ± 0.31) mRNAs are enriched in the Ntf3 cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: WFS1 is expressed specifically in several structures in the adult mouse brain that are relevant to stress and depression, including superficial layers of the cerebral cortex, the central extended area of the amygdala, and pyramidal cells in the CA1 field of the hippocampus.
source: As expected, WFS1 is expressed specifically in several structures in the adult mouse brain that are relevant to stress and depression, including superficial layers of the cerebral cortex, the central extended area of the amygdala (data not shown), and pyramidal cells in the CA1 field of the hippocampus (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: WFS1 is co-expressed with Ntf3 in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells of the PFC.
source: Although WFS1 is clearly co-expressed with Ntf3 in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells of the PFC (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: WFS1 expression is entirely distinct from Ntf3 expression in the hippocampus.
source: its expression is entirely distinct from Ntf3 expression in the hippocampus (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: WFS1 is an ER membrane protein.
source: WFS1 is an ER membrane protein (Takeda et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takeda et al., 2001.

claim: WFS1 is thought to be important in Ca2+ homeostasis.
source: that is thought to be important in Ca2+ homeostasis (Yurimoto et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yurimoto et al., 2009.

claim: WFS1 is thought to be important in insulin secretion.
source: insulin secretion (Ishihara et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishihara et al., 2004.

claim: WFS1 is thought to be important in the unfolded protein response.
source: and the unfolded protein response (Fonseca et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fonseca et al., 2005.

claim: Dense staining of the ER was observed in all cortical cells that were positive for WFS1, principally in the cell soma and primary dendrites.
source: Consistent with ultrastructural studies of peripheral and cultured cell types, dense staining of the ER was observed in all cortical cells that were positive for WFS1, principally in the cell soma and primary dendrites (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A Wfs1-mutant mouse line carrying a conditional allele (Wfs1 F/F) was generated by targeting loxP sites surrounding the eighth and largest exon of the gene.
source: Accordingly, we generated a Wfs1-mutant mouse line carrying a conditional allele (Wfs1 F/F) by targeting loxP sites surrounding the eighth and largest exon of the gene (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own description of their mouse generation strategy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Exon 8 of Wfs1 encodes the C-terminal hydrophilic domain, the site of many nonsense, and missense mutations that cause Wolfram Syndrome.
source: This exon was chosen because it encodes the C-terminal hydrophilic domain, the site of many nonsense, and missense mutations that cause Wolfram Syndrome (Rigoli et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rigoli et al., 2011.

claim: The Emx1.IRES.cre driver line expresses the Cre recombinase specifically in the telencephalon.
source: To remove WFS1 from the cerebral cortex, we employed the Emx1.IRES.cre driver line that expresses the Cre recombinase specifically in the telencephalon (Figure 3B) (Gorski et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gorski et al., 2002 and the authors' own data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Important subcortical sites of Wfs1 expression, including the amygdala, striatum, and hypothalamus, are unaffected in Emx1.IRES.cre driver line.
source: Important subcortical sites of Wfs1 expression, including the amygdala, striatum, and hypothalamus (Luuk et al., 2008), are unaffected in Emx1.IRES.cre driver line (Figure 3B; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Luuk et al., 2008.

claim: Emx1 is expressed in all forebrain excitatory neurons and glia.
source: Furthermore, although previous studies indicate that Emx1 is expressed in all forebrain excitatory neurons and glia
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies, though not specifically cited.

claim: Wfs1 expression is restricted to layer 2/3 cortical pyramidal cells and CA1 hippocampal neurons in forebrain structures.
source: the fact that Wfs1 expression is restricted to layer 2/3 cortical pyramidal cells and CA1 hippocampal neurons in forebrain structures indicates that any phenotypes evident in Wfs1 telencephalon-specific conditional knockout mice (Wfs1/CKO) generated by conditional deletion of Wolframin using the Emx1.IRES.cre driver line must result from loss of function in these excitatory neuron populations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' expression data and the properties of the Emx1.IRES.cre driver line.

claim: Wfs1/CKO mice were born in normal Mendelian ratio.
source: Wfs1/CKO mice were born in normal Mendelian ratio
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own observations of breeding outcomes.

claim: Wfs1/CKO mice had normal ad libitum body weight compared with their wild-type (wt) littermates.
source: and had normal ad libitum body weight compared with their wild-type (wt) littermates.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own measurements.

claim: Glucose levels were normal in Wfs1/CKO mice as assessed by urinalysis in non-fasting conditions.
source: Glucose levels were normal in these mice as assessed by urinalysis in non-fasting conditions (data not shown)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own data, though not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Emx1 is exclusively expressed in the CNS.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies showing that Emx1 is exclusively expressed in the CNS (Gorski et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gorski et al., 2002.

claim: Wfs1/CKO mice carrying both the floxed allele and the Emx1.IRES.cre driver lost all detectable WFS1 expression in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.
source: As expected, Wfs1/CKO mice carrying both the floxed allele and the Emx1.IRES.cre driver exhibited wt expression of WFS1 in all subcortical structures, but lost all detectable WFS1 expression in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus (Figure 3B, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Patients with Wolfram syndrome exhibit enhanced sensitivity to stress and depression.
source: The specific loss of Wfs1 in the forebrain of Wfs1/CKO mice presented an important opportunity to determine whether the enhanced sensitivity to stress and depression of patients with Wolfram syndrome (Koido et al., 2005; Swift and Swift, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Koido et al., 2005; Swift and Swift, 2005).

claim: Wfs1 KO mice display behavioral abnormalities.
source: or the behavioral abnormalities of Wfs1 KO mice (Kato et al., 2008; Luuk et al., 2009), might result from abnormal function of forebrain neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Kato et al., 2008; Luuk et al., 2009).

claim: Acute psychological stressors such as swim stress and ARS strongly alter rodent behavior in the FST and in the sucrose preference test (SPT).
source: Acute psychological stressors such as swim stress and ARS strongly alter rodent behavior in the FST and in the sucrose preference test (SPT) (Duncan et al., 1993; Cullinan et al., 1995; Jankord and Herman, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Duncan et al., 1993; Cullinan et al., 1995; Jankord and Herman, 2008).

claim: The FST and SPT are designed to measure two hallmarks of depression, behavioral despair, and anhedonia.
source: These tests are designed to measure two hallmarks of depression, behavioral despair, and anhedonia
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about these behavioral assays.

claim: The effect of ARS on FST and SPT behaviors in rodents has been used to model the effects of acute stress on depression.
source: and the effect of ARS on these behaviors in rodents has been used to model the effects of acute stress on depression (Kohda et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kohda et al., 2007.

claim: Deletion of Wfs1 from forebrain neurons in Wfs1/CKO mice revealed no differences in behavior under normal baseline conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 3, deletion of Wfs1 from forebrain neurons in Wfs1/CKO mice revealed no differences in behavior under normal baseline conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Wfs1/CKO mice displayed a significant increase in immobility in the FST after exposure to ARS.
source: Thus, Wfs1/CKO mice displayed a significant increase in immobility in the FST (Figure 3C; Two-way analysis of variance [ANOVA]—Bonferroni post hoc test: CKO Basal vs CKO + ARS, p < 0.05*, n = 8 per group)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: Wfs1/CKO mice displayed a strong decrease in sucrose preference after exposure to ARS stress.
source: and a strong decrease in sucrose preference after exposure to ARS stress (Figure 3D; Two-way ANOVA—Bonferroni post hoc test: CKO Basal vs CKO + ARS, p < 0.001**, n = 10 per group).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of Wfs1 in the cortex and hippocampus does not disrupt baseline learning or cognitive flexibility.
source: Our results indicate, therefore, that loss of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons does not disrupt baseline learning or cognitive flexibility
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' behavioral data showing normal performance in learning assays.

claim: Loss of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons renders the animals vulnerable to stress-induced depression-related behaviors.
source: but renders the animals vulnerable to stress-induced depression-related behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' behavioral data showing enhanced depressive behaviors after stress.

claim: The mPFC is altered in response to stress.
source: previous studies have shown that the mPFC is both altered in response to stress (Radley et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Radley et al., 2004.

claim: The mPFC is important for behavioral resilience in response to stress under a variety of conditions.
source: and important for behavioral resilience in response to stress under a variety of conditions (Warden et al., 2012; Maier, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Warden et al., 2012; Maier, 2015).

claim: AAV2 expressing Cre recombinase was injected into the mPFC of homozygous mutant mice (Wfs1 F/F) to generate Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice.
source: Specifically, we injected an AAV2 expressing Cre recombinase tagged at the N-terminus with EYFP (AAV2.CMV.HI.GFP-Cre.SV40) into the mPFC of homozygous mutant mice (Wfs1 F/F) and generated Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own description of their experimental procedure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wfs1 expression is efficiently deleted on the side of the mPFC that was injected with AAV2.CMV.HI.GFP-Cre.SV40.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, Wfs1 (red) continues to be expressed in the side of mPFC that has not received the virus, whereas Wfs1 expression is efficiently deleted on the side of the mPFC that was injected with AAV2.CMV.HI.GFP-Cre.SV40.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is no loss of Wfs1 expression in cortices injected with the control virus.
source: Although the use of intersectional viral approaches must necessarily result in some differences in the precise number and exact locations of the infected cells, examination of data from many animals indicated that there is no loss of Wfs1 expression in cortices injected with the control virus (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of Wfs1 in response to injection of the Cre-expressing virus was regional and reproducible.
source: whereas loss of Wfs1 in response to injection of the Cre-expressing virus was regional and reproducible (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There were no differences between control and Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice in any of the measured behaviors under normal baseline conditions.
source: As expected, there were no differences between control and Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice in any of the measured behaviors, including the behavioral despair and anhedonia assays, under normal baseline conditions (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Exposure of Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice to ARS resulted in increased immobility in the FST.
source: However, exposure of Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice to ARS resulted specifically in enhanced responses to stress, including increased immobility in the FST (Figure 4E; Two-way ANOVA—Bonferroni post hoc test: mPFC.KO Basal vs mPFC.KO + ARS, p < 0.01**, N = 8 per group)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 4E with statistical analysis.

claim: Exposure of Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice to ARS resulted in suppressed preference for sucrose.
source: and suppressed preference for sucrose (Figure 4F; Two-way ANOVA—Bonferroni post hoc test: C + ARS vs mPFC.KO + ARS: p < 0.01**, N = 7 per group).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 4F with statistical analysis.

claim: Spontaneous locomotion is not aberrant in the Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice after exposure to ARS.
source: Spontaneous locomotion (Figure 4G) and anxiety-related behavior (Figure 4H) are not aberrant in the Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice after exposure to ARS.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Anxiety-related behavior is not aberrant in the Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice after exposure to ARS.
source: Spontaneous locomotion (Figure 4G) and anxiety-related behavior (Figure 4H) are not aberrant in the Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice after exposure to ARS.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Wfs1 function is required in the mPFC for layer 2/3 pyramidal cells to respond normally to stress.
source: These data are consistent with those obtained from forebrain deletion of Wfs1 in the Wfs1/CKO animals (Figure 3C,D) and extend those observations to allow the conclusion that Wfs1 function is required in the mPFC for layer 2/3 pyramidal cells to respond normally to stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' behavioral data from both Wfs1/CKO and Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells may be an important nexus for exploration of molecular mechanisms that contribute to the comorbidity of stress and depression in human populations.
source: The observation that depressive behaviors are enhanced specifically in these mice strongly suggests that layer 2/3 pyramidal cells may be an important nexus for exploration of molecular mechanisms that contribute to the comorbidity of stress and depression in human populations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the authors' data extrapolated to human populations.

claim: Patients with Wolfram syndrome display altered stress responses.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that both patients with Wolfram syndrome and Wfs1 knockout mice display altered stress responses (Sequeira et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sequeira et al., 2003.

claim: Wfs1 knockout mice display elevated levels of serum corticosterone upon exposure to stress.
source: including elevated levels of serum corticosterone upon exposure to stress (Kato et al., 2008; Luuk et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Kato et al., 2008; Luuk et al., 2009).

claim: ARS resulted in significantly higher levels of cFos activation in the hypothalamic PVN of Wfs1/CKO mice compared with controls.
source: As shown in Figure 5, ARS resulted in significantly higher levels of cFos activation in the hypothalamic PVN of Wfs1/CKO mice compared with controls (Figure 5A,B) (Two-way ANOVA—Bonferroni post hoc test: WT + ARS vs CKO + ARS, p < 0.001***, N = 3 per group).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A,B with statistical analysis.

claim: Baseline corticosterone levels were not different in wt and Wfs1/CKO mice.
source: These experiments revealed that baseline corticosterone levels were not different in wt and Wfs1/CKO mice (WT: 46.17 ± 5.00; CKO: 55.26 ± 10.18)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own radioimmunoassay data.

claim: In both wt and Wfs1/CKO serum corticosterone levels increased in response to stress.
source: and that in both wt and Wfs1/CKO serum corticosterone levels increased in response to stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own radioimmunoassay data.

claim: The magnitude of the increase of serum corticosterone observed in Wfs1/CKO in response to stress was significantly greater than that seen in their wt littermates.
source: However, the magnitude of the increase of serum corticosterone observed in Wfs1/CKO in response to stress (CKO + ARS: 505.12 ± 7.63) was significantly greater than that seen in their wt littermates (WT + ARS: 401.50 ± 6.00) (Two-way ANOVA—Bonferroni post hoc test: WT + ARS vs CKO + ARS, p < 0.001***, N = 5 per group).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own radioimmunoassay data with statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons causes hyperactivation of the PVN and the HPA axis in response to stress.
source: We conclude, therefore, that loss of Wfs1 in forebrain neurons causes hyperactivation of the PVN and the HPA axis in response to stress (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' data on cFos activation and corticosterone levels.

claim: Normal responses to stressful stimuli require the function of Wfs1 in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the mPFC.
source: Taken together with the enhanced behavioral responses of Wfs1/CKO and Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice to ARS, these results demonstrate that normal responses to stressful stimuli require the function of Wfs1 in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the mPFC (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined behavioral and physiological data from the authors' experiments.

claim: Dysfunction in Wfs1-expressing pyramidal cells in the mPFC may contribute to MDD as a result of enhanced susceptibility to stress.
source: Given the identification of Wfs1 as a genetic cause of MDD (Flint and Kendler, 2014) and previous studies demonstrating that behavioral resilience requires normal function of the mPFC (Russo et al., 2012), our data provide strong evidence that dysfunction in Wfs1-expressing pyramidal cells in the mPFC may contribute to MDD as a result of enhanced susceptibility to stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the authors' data in the context of human MDD.

claim: Wfs1-expressing cells in the mPFC project within the cortex and to the caudate putamen.
source: As shown in Figure 6, Wfs1-expressing neurons in the mPFC project locally within the mPFC, and across the corpus callosum to the contralateral primary motor cortex. These neurons also project subcortically through the pyramidal tract to terminate in the caudate putamen (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own viral tracing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Wfs1 pyramidal cells receive afferent information from pyramidal cells spanning several layers and regions of the cerebral cortex.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, our results demonstrate that Wfs1 pyramidal cells receive afferent information from pyramidal cells spanning several layers and regions of the cerebral cortex
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own rabies virus tracing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Projection neurons in the posterior thalamic nuclear group (Po) synapse onto Wfs1-expressing cells in the mPFC.
source: and that projection neurons in the posterior thalamic nuclear group (Po) and the lateral amygdala synapse onto Wfs1-expressing cells in the mPFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own rabies virus tracing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Projection neurons in the lateral amygdala synapse onto Wfs1-expressing cells in the mPFC.
source: and that projection neurons in the posterior thalamic nuclear group (Po) and the lateral amygdala synapse onto Wfs1-expressing cells in the mPFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own rabies virus tracing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: WFS1 is localized in the ER and participates in a regulatory pathway that negatively regulates ER stress signaling.
source: Studies of WFS1 localization and function in the pancreas have demonstrated that WFS1 is present in the ER, and thus it participates in a regulatory pathway that negatively regulates ER stress signaling (Fonseca et al., 2010; Oslowski and Urano, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Fonseca et al., 2010; Oslowski and Urano, 2011).

claim: In the absence of Wfs1, pancreatic β cells are unable to adjust to changing glucose levels, resulting in altered β-cell function, apoptosis, and pancreatic degeneration.
source: In the absence of Wfs1, pancreatic β cells are unable to adjust to changing glucose levels, resulting in altered β-cell function, apoptosis, and pancreatic degeneration (Ishihara et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishihara et al., 2004.

claim: TRAP translational profiling of Ntf3 cortical cells demonstrated significant enrichment of the mRNAs for WNT7A and NTF3.
source: TRAP translational profiling of Ntf3 cortical cells (Figure 1G) demonstrated significant enrichment of the mRNAs for several secreted proteins that are of interest because of their known roles in neuronal function, including wingless-related MMTV integration site 7a (WNT7A) and neurotrophin 3 (NTF3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own TRAP profiling data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: No differences were evident in WNT7A, NTF3, or BDNF from wt or Wfs1/CKO animals under baseline conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 7, no differences were evident in any of these proteins from wt or Wfs1/CKO animals under baseline conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In response to ARS, the abundance of WNT7A and NTF3 were both altered in Wfs1/CKO animals.
source: However, in response to ARS, the abundance of WNT7A and NTF3 were both altered.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: WNT7A is a secreted signaling factor that is involved in axonal remodeling and synaptic differentiation.
source: WNT7A is a secreted signaling factor that is involved in axonal remodeling and synaptic differentiation (Ciani et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ciani et al., 2011.

claim: In Wfs1/CKO animals, WNT7A is specifically decreased in the PFC in response to ARS.
source: In Wfs1/CKO animals, it is specifically decreased in the PFC (Two-way ANOVA—Bonferroni post hoc test: CKO Basal vs CKO + ARS, p < 0.001**, N = 3 per group) (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own Western blot data shown in Figure 7A with statistical analysis.

claim: Mature NTF3 (∼14 kDa) is processed from a ∼32-kDa precursor that is referred to as proNTF3.
source: Mature NTF3 (∼14 kDa) is processed from a ∼32-kDa precursor that is referred to as proNTF3 (Yano et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yano et al., 2009.

claim: Increased levels of proNTF3 were consistently observed in Wfs1 knockout animals in response to ARS.
source: Although we could not reliably detect mature NTF3 on Western blots from PFC, increased levels of proNTF3 were consistently observed in Wfs1 knockout animals in response to ARS (Two-way ANOVA—Bonferroni post hoc test: CKO Basal vs CKO + ARS, p < 0.0001***, N = 3 per group) (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own Western blot data shown in Figure 7B with statistical analysis.

claim: Changes in WNT7A and proNTF3 were not observed in hippocampal neurons extracts processed from the same animals.
source: These changes were not observed in hippocampal neurons extracts processed from the same animals (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own Western blot data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: No changes in BDNF were evident in Western blots prepared from either the PFC or hippocampus (HPC) in response to loss of Wfs1.
source: No changes in BDNF were evident in Western blots prepared from either the PFC or hippocampus (HPC) in response to loss of Wfs1 (Figure 7C,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own Western blot data shown in Figure 7C,F.

claim: Processing and release of growth factors, neurotrophins and perhaps other secreted proteins are disturbed in layer 2/3 neurons harboring Wfs1 deletion.
source: These data demonstrate that processing and release of growth factors, neurotrophins and perhaps other secreted proteins are disturbed in layer 2/3 neurons harboring Wfs1 deletion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' Western blot data showing altered WNT7A and proNTF3 levels.

claim: MDD is a behaviorally and genetically complex disorder that is thought to arise from dysfunction in a distributed circuit involving the mPFC, the anterior cingulate cortex, the striatum, the thalamus, and other brain areas.
source: MDD is a behaviorally and genetically complex disorder that that is thought to arise from dysfunction in a distributed circuit involving the mPFC, the anterior cingulate cortex, the striatum, the thalamus, and other brain areas (Russo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2012.

claim: Wfs1 is co-expressed with Ntf3, Penk, and Wnt7a in supragranular 2/3 pyramidal neurons in the mPFC.
source: Here, we report that Wfs1, a gene that can cause depression (Flint and Kendler, 2014), is co-expressed with Ntf3, Penk, and Wnt7a in supragranular 2/3 pyramidal neurons in the mPFC.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own TRAP profiling and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Conditional deletion of Wfs1 from the forebrain results in the induction of depressive behaviors in response to acute stress.
source: We demonstrate that conditional deletion of Wfs1 from the forebrain in general, or from the mPFC specifically, results in the induction of depressive behaviors in response to acute stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data from Wfs1/CKO and Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice.

claim: Conditional deletion of Wfs1 from the mPFC results in the induction of depressive behaviors in response to acute stress.
source: We demonstrate that conditional deletion of Wfs1 from the forebrain in general, or from the mPFC specifically, results in the induction of depressive behaviors in response to acute stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own behavioral data from Wfs1 mPFC.KO mice.

claim: Conditional deletion of Wfs1 is accompanied by hyperactivation of the HPA axis and elevation of serum corticosterone.
source: This is accompanied by hyperactivation of the HPA axis and elevation of serum corticosterone.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own data on cFos activation and corticosterone levels.

claim: Wolframin is localized to the ER in superficial cortical pyramidal cells.
source: We show that Wolframin (the protein encoded by Wfs1) is localized to the ER in these neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the mPFC are a crucial node in the circuitry regulating depressive behaviors in response to stress.
source: We conclude that layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the mPFC are a crucial node in the circuitry regulating depressive behaviors in response to stress
evidence: The claim is inferred from the authors' combined behavioral, physiological, and molecular data.

claim: Identification of mechanisms that regulate the activity of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons and their downstream targets can provide important insights into the relationship between stress and depression.
source: and that identification of mechanisms that regulate the activity of these neurons, and their downstream targets can provide important insights into the relationship between stress and depression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions based on the authors' findings.

claim: Heterozygous carriers of mutant Wfs1 alleles exhibit clinical features of pure MDD.
source: Heterozygous carriers of mutant Wfs1 alleles are also affected, exhibiting clinical features of pure MDD.
evidence: This reflects established clinical knowledge about Wfs1 carriers.

claim: As many as 7% of the patients hospitalized for MDD may be predisposed due to Wfs1 mutations.
source: It has been estimated that as many as 7% of the patients hospitalized for MDD may be predisposed due to Wfs1 mutations (Swift et al., 1990; Crawford et al., 2002; Swift and Swift, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Swift et al., 1990; Crawford et al., 2002; Swift and Swift, 2005).

claim: Wfs1 knockout mice display impaired behavioral adaptation to stress.
source: Studies of Wfs1 knockout mice have shown that they replicate central and peripheral features of Wolfram syndrome and that they display impaired behavioral adaptation to stress (Sequeira et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2008; Luuk et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Sequeira et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2008; Luuk et al., 2009).

claim: WFS1 tightly controls ER stress to regulate insulin production in response to frequent fluctuations of blood glucose in pancreatic β cells.
source: In the case of pancreatic β cells, it is thought that WFS1 tightly controls ER stress to regulate insulin production in response to frequent fluctuations of blood glucose.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about WFS1 function in pancreatic β cells.

claim: WNT7A has clear positive roles in synapse formation and maintenance.
source: Clear positive roles for WNT7A in synapse formation and maintenance have been documented in several systems (Hall et al., 2000; Gogolla et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Hall et al., 2000; Gogolla et al., 2009).

claim: NTF3 has an important trophic role in synapse formation.
source: In contrast to NTF3, which has an important trophic role in synapse formation
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about NTF3 function.

claim: proNTF3 can induce apoptosis in cultured cells, suggesting a negative role for proNTF3 in neurons.
source: proNTF3 can induce apoptosis in cultured cells, suggesting a negative role for proNTF3 in neurons (Yano et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yano et al., 2009.

claim: Receptors for glucocorticoid (Nr3c1), estrogen (Esr1), and adrenergic receptors (Adra2c, Adr2a and Adrb1) are expressed in Wfs1-positive cells in the cortex.
source: We find that receptors for three circulating factors that are important for stress responsivity are expressed in Wfs1-positive cells in the cortex: Nr3c1, the glucocorticoid receptor; Esr1, the estrogen receptor; and several adrenergic receptors, Adra2c, Adr2a and Adrb1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own expression data, likely from TRAP profiling.

claim: Wfs1-expressing cells in the mPFC receive input from several adjacent cortical regions, from the BLA and from the thalamus.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6, Wfs1-expressing cells in the mPFC receive input from several adjacent cortical regions, from the BLA and from the thalamus.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' own viral tracing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Loss of Wfs1 in mPFC impairs signaling to the striatum.
source: Thus far, our data have demonstrated projections from Wfs1-expressing cells primarily to neighboring and contralateral cortical structures, and to the caudate putamen. Given the central role that striatal circuits play in both stress and depression, the simplest interpretation of our results is that loss of Wfs1 in mPFC impairs signaling to the striatum
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the authors' tracing and behavioral data.

claim: Failure to stimulate GABAergic output from the NAc to the PVN is responsible for hyperactivation of the HPA axis in this model of stress-induced depression.
source: and that failure to stimulate GABAergic output from the NAc to the PVN (Russo et al., 2012) is responsible for hyperactivation of the HPA axis in this model of stress-induced depression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the authors' data based on a citation to Russo et al., 2012.

claim: Genetic studies indicating an association between MDD and bipolar disorder and Wfs1 have not been consistently confirmed.
source: Although genetic studies indicating an association between MDD and bipolar disorder and Wfs1 have not been consistently confirmed (Ohtsuki et al., 2000; Koido et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Ohtsuki et al., 2000; Koido et al., 2005).

claim: Investigation of Wfs1 carriers and family members has provided strong evidence that Wfs1 mutations can lead to an increased incidence of psychiatric admissions for hospitalization.
source: investigation of Wfs1 carriers and family members has provided strong evidence that Wfs1 mutations can lead to an increased incidence of psychiatric admissions for hospitalization (Swift et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swift et al., 1991.

claim: Further investigation of layer 2/3 cells in other models of depression, and in response to a variety of stressors, can shed important new light on pathways that operate in these cells to moderate depressive behaviors in response to stressful environments.
source: Given the important contributions that family studies have made to our understanding of disease (Pohodich and Zoghbi, 2015), we believe that further investigation of layer 2/3 cells in other models of depression, and in response to a variety of stressors, can shed important new light on pathways that operate in these cells to moderate depressive behaviors in response to stressful environments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions based on the authors' findings and a citation to Pohodich and Zoghbi, 2015.
